week_1.text:
We just shipped something most ad platforms won't build for years.

Synter now has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server — meaning any AI agent (Claude, Cursor, Amp) can manage your ad campaigns across 7 platforms through a single interface.

What that looks like in practice:

→ Ask Claude to pull your Google Ads performance
→ Have it pause underperforming Meta campaigns
→ Reallocate budget to your best LinkedIn ad sets
→ Generate fresh creatives with Imagen 4
→ Launch everything — without opening a single dashboard

For agencies managing multiple clients across platforms, this means your media buyers spend less time in dashboards and more time on strategy.

The MCP server handles OAuth credential injection, credit billing, user scoping, and audit logging automatically. Your AI agent just talks to Synter, and Synter executes.

This is what we mean by AI Agent Media Buyers. Not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. An execution layer that gives your team their time back.

Try it → syntermedia.ai/developer

week_1.text:
The average media buyer manages 3-4 platforms manually.

They log into Google Ads. Pull a report. Switch to Meta. Pull another report. Open a spreadsheet. Compare numbers. Make a decision. Go back to each platform. Adjust bids. Repeat.

That workflow takes 6-8 hours per week — and it's fundamentally reactive. By the time you've analyzed yesterday's data across platforms, the opportunity has already moved.

Here's the shift we're seeing:

The best agencies are splitting the work differently. Strategy stays with the human. Execution goes to AI agents.

An AI agent pulls performance from all 7 platforms simultaneously. It identifies the cross-platform pattern — "LinkedIn CPL dropped 22% while Google CPA rose 15% on the same audience" — and acts on it in minutes, not days.

This isn't about replacing media buyers. It's about giving them agents that handle execution so they can focus on what they were hired for: strategic thinking.

The teams that figure this out first will operate at a fundamentally different speed.

week_1.text:
March build update — shipping faster than ever.

What we deployed in the last 30 days:

→ Reddit Ads v3 API integration (full campaign lifecycle)
→ SimilarWeb competitive intelligence via MCP
→ X Growth Engine with pay-per-usage ads API
→ TikTok Events API for server-side conversion tracking
→ Microsoft Ads offline conversions
→ Granular OAuth connection UX with 10-stage progress tracking

The hardest bug this month: Reddit's OAuth endpoint silently drops your refresh_token when PKCE code_challenge is present. No error. No warning. Your connection just dies after 60 minutes.

We patched our Nango instance to disable PKCE for Reddit specifically. Took 3 days to diagnose, 4 lines to fix.

Building ad platform integrations is 20% feature work and 80% debugging undocumented API behavior.

Every integration we build is one less platform a media buyer needs to context-switch into.

More coming next week.

week_1.text:
Why the best media buyers are adopting AI agents (and it's not why you think)

I keep hearing the same concern from agency owners: "AI is going to replace my team."

After spending 6 months building Synter and talking to dozens of agencies, I can tell you the opposite is happening.

The best media buyers — the ones running $50K+ across 5 platforms for demanding clients — are the ones most excited about AI agents.

Not because they want to be replaced. Because they're exhausted.

Here's the reality nobody talks about:

A senior media buyer managing 5 clients across Google, Meta, LinkedIn, Reddit, and TikTok has roughly 25 dashboard sessions per day. Each session involves logging in, pulling data, making a decision, executing that decision, and documenting it.

That's not strategy. That's data entry with a fancy job title.

The burnout is real. The mistakes that come from context-switching between platforms all day are real. The opportunity cost of spending 80% of your time on execution is real.

What AI agents actually change:

→ Campaign creation goes from 45 minutes to 90 seconds
→ Cross-platform reporting goes from 2 hours to one sentence
→ Budget reallocation across platforms goes from 30 minutes per platform to one command
→ Conversion tracking setup goes from a manual hour to automatic

That's 15+ hours per week back. Per media buyer. Per client.

What do they do with that time? The thing they were actually hired for: understanding the customer, developing creative strategy, testing new channels, building competitive moats.

The agencies I see thriving aren't replacing people. They're giving their people better tools so they can do higher-value work.

The ones that figure this out first will be able to serve more clients, with better results, without burning out their team.

That's what we're building at Synter.

week_2.text:
Here's how Synter manages a $50/day Google Ads campaign from a single chat message.

The prompt: "Create a search campaign for SaaS lead gen targeting marketing automation keywords with a $50 daily budget."

What Synter does in under 90 seconds:

1. Creates the campaign with all Google Ads API v21 required fields
2. Sets bidding to maximize_clicks (no conversion data yet — Synter knows not to use maximize_conversions without tracking)
3. Generates keyword groups from the prompt
4. Creates responsive search ads with 15 headlines and 4 descriptions
5. Sets geo-targeting
6. Launches in PAUSED state for review

Then, without being asked:

→ Creates a Google Ads conversion action
→ Sets up the GTM tag with the conversion label
→ Publishes the GTM container
→ Recommends switching to maximize_conversions after 15-30 conversions

No dashboard hopping. No copy-pasting conversion IDs between tabs. No forgetting to publish the GTM container (we've all done it).

The media buyer reviews in 2 minutes, approves, enables. Done.

That's what AI Agent Media Buyers actually means. Your strategist still makes the call. The agent handles the 47 clicks.

week_2.text:
The agency model isn't broken. The tools are.

I keep seeing hot takes about how AI will kill agencies. That's wrong.

Agencies exist because businesses need strategic marketing expertise. That need isn't going away. What's going away is the inefficiency.

Right now, a typical agency allocates roughly:
• 20% of billable hours on strategy and creative
• 30% on campaign setup and management
• 25% on reporting and data analysis
• 25% on client communication and coordination

The 55% spent on setup, management, and reporting is where AI agents create leverage. Not by replacing the agency, but by compressing that work so dramatically that the same team can:

→ Serve more clients without hiring
→ Spend more time on the strategic work that justifies premium pricing
→ Test more platforms and creative angles per client
→ Reduce execution mistakes from context-switching

The agencies that adopt AI execution tools will out-deliver and out-margin agencies that don't.

Not because their strategy is better. Because their strategists actually have time to strategize.

That's the unlock.

week_2.text:
The hidden cost of being spread too thin in paid media (and what to do about it)

Every media buyer I talk to describes the same problem differently:

"I don't have time to test TikTok."
"I know Reddit would work for this client but I can't add another dashboard."
"We stopped running LinkedIn because nobody had bandwidth."

The common thread: it's never a strategy problem. It's a capacity problem.

When you're managing Google and Meta all day, every additional platform isn't just another dashboard. It's another set of:

→ Bid strategies to learn
→ Audience targeting logic to understand
→ Creative specs to master
→ Reporting formats to normalize
→ API quirks to debug

So platforms get cut. Not because they wouldn't work, but because there literally aren't enough hours.

The math is brutal:

A media buyer spending 8 hours/day managing 3 platforms has zero capacity for platform #4. Even if platform #4 would deliver 30% lower CPA.

This is the opportunity cost nobody measures. The campaigns you never ran. The audiences you never tested. The creative angles you never explored.

Because you were too busy checking bid caps.

What AI agents change:

When execution is handled by agents, adding a platform goes from "hire someone" to "ask the agent." The strategic decision (should we test Reddit for this client?) stays with the human. The execution (create campaign, set targeting, write copy, track conversions) goes to the agent.

The result isn't replacing media buyers. It's un-bottlenecking them.

The agencies that figure this out will test more, learn faster, and deliver better results. Not because they have more people. Because their people have more time.

That's what we're building at Synter. One interface. Every platform. You direct, they execute.

week_3.text:
The execution gap: why good strategy fails in paid media

I've been thinking about a pattern I see over and over in advertising.

Someone hires a great strategist. The strategy is sound. The target audience is well-defined. The creative brief is sharp. The channel mix makes sense.

And then it underperforms.

Not because the strategy was wrong. Because the execution was compromised.

Here's how it happens:

The media buyer who implements the strategy is also implementing strategies for 4 other clients. They're managing Google, Meta, and LinkedIn for each. That's 15 active dashboards.

By Wednesday, they're behind on reporting for Client A, which means they rush the campaign setup for Client B. A geo target gets set wrong. A bid cap gets left on auto. A negative keyword list doesn't get applied.

Small mistakes. But they compound.

After a month, the strategist looks at the numbers and says "the strategy didn't work." But the strategy was never properly executed. It was executed by someone who was spread too thin to get the details right.

This is the execution gap. And it's the single biggest source of wasted ad spend that nobody tracks.

You can't A/B test strategy vs. execution. You can't attribute a wrong geo target to a line item in your P&L. You can't measure the campaigns you would have run if your team had more bandwidth.

But you can close the gap.

When execution is handled by AI agents:

→ Campaign settings are applied consistently, every time
→ Negative keywords get added the moment they're identified
→ Budget changes happen in seconds, not "I'll get to it after this client call"
→ Conversion tracking doesn't get forgotten because it's automatic
→ New platforms get tested because adding one is a sentence, not a project

The strategist's job doesn't change. But their strategy actually gets executed as designed.

That's the real unlock. Not better strategy. Not better creative. Better execution of the strategy and creative you already have.

At Synter, we're building the execution layer that closes this gap. One interface. Every platform. You direct, they execute.
